newsitem.title: UK: Dlr to gun for 120 yen, helped by Asia currency crisis.
newsitem.headline: Dlr to gun for 120 yen, helped by Asia currency crisis.

text.p: The dollar will head towards 120 yen as dealers put Japanese interest rate rise expectations on hold and worry that the Asian currency crisis will hurt the fledgling Japanese recovery, analysts said on Friday.
When the South East Asian forex turmoil started in May with a speculative attack on the Thai baht, things looked more upbeat for the yen.
The main catalyst for its rise then was a sharp revision of interest rate expectations, helped by a rising trade surplus. The yen also benefited from its perceived safe-haven status in the region.
But neither equation holds true any more, analysts said.

"The mood about Japan has become more gloomy, and in such a climate continued pressure on South East Asian currencies is adding to worries about Japan's competitiveness," said Tim Fox, chief treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.
Signs in late spring that Japan was emerging from the doldrums fueled speculation that the official discount rate would be raised from its record low 0.50 percent.

The result was that the yen rose in early June to a high of 110.52 per dollar, a level not seen since November 1996. It also gained strongly against the mark as expectations of German interest rate rises were still dormant.

Since then, traders have become less confident about Japan's economy amid disappointment about the patchy nature of its recovery and revised their expectations for a rate rise to later this year or early in 1998.

The International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday Japan should keep a lid on short-term interest to give its economic revival a chance. Japan should maintain its easy monetary stance for now and begin tightening later in the year, the IMF said.
U.S. data, meanwhile, continue to paint a picture of economic growth with low inflation, a holy-grail scenario for risk-adverse investors.
And the mark's attractiveness has increased after the Bundesbank's warnings about inflation fueled speculation that German credit might be tightened soon.

With a large part of South East Asia gaining a competitive advantage from their tumbling currencies, concern is increasing about Japanese exporters' ability to compete there after the currency turmoil spread across the region.
The latest victim was the Indonesian rupiah, which tumbled to record lows against the dollar after it was floated on Thursday.

"There's a general trend of Asian currencies showing a lot of volatility at the moment, and as a result, their weakening makes the yen look rather overvalued relative to all those currencies, and the yen needs to weaken for competitive reasons," said James Binney, fund manager at GNI in London.

"Most of those east Asian currencies were effectively pegged to the dollar, and now they're falling relative to the dollar. So the issue has more to do with dollar/yen rather than mark/yen, though obviously it will have an impact on all the yen crosses," said Binney.

Kit Juckes, currency strategist at NatWest Markets here, said even though China and Hong Kong were the more important trading partners for Japan, the possible impact on Japanese exports could not be ignored.
"The yen's weakness is due to more than just one factor but it's hard to see anything positive for the yen out of the Asian currency crisis," said Juckes.
A large holding of Thailand's foreign debt by Japanese banks has not helped the yen, analysts said. Major Japanese banks are also heavily exposed to other Asian nations.
Japan pledged this week to take a fourth of the burden of a global $16 billion bailout scheme for Thailand to ease its credit problems and prevent a regional chain reaction.
Analysts said money moving out of the Asian region was going into the United States where the economy is performing much better than that of Japan.

A drop in the yield of Japan's benchmark long bond to a record low 2.065 percent overnight increased the yield advantage of U.S. assets even further. The long U.S. Treasury bond yields around 6.55 percent at present.
The dollar rose to a two-week high of 118.70 in Europe on Friday and traded at 118.45/55 at 1155 GMT, up from around 114.60 at the start of the European week.
All eyes are focusing again on the 120-yen level because of its sensitivity in trade relations between the U.S. and Japan.
As dollar/yen approaches 120, Japanese authorities are likely to resort to rhetoric, at least, about possible central bank intervention to stem the yen's decline, analysts said.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see dollar/yen at 120 again soon but that will meet with the usual jawboning out of Japan," said Juckes.
